digest.intro: Infrastructure cracks, chip rules bend, and dead stars pulse wrong.

items.title: Lutnick Is Writing Chip Rules That Benefit His Sons' Clients
items.blurb: A Malaysian data center called A201 — client of Cantor Fitzgerald, now run by Howard Lutnick's sons — is about to open packed with Nvidia's most advanced AI servers, supplying compute to a Chinese tech giant through a legal loophole. Lutnick, as Commerce Secretary, has been the internal force slowing rules that would close that loophole. Treasury's Bessent confronted him directly; Senate testimony is now being called for.

items.title: Trump-Xi-Putin Trilateral, Tankers Mined at Hormuz, Bahrain Strike
items.blurb: Three interlocking events landed simultaneously: Iran's IRGC says two oil tankers struck naval mines south of the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire (commercial transits reportedly down 80% from baseline), IRGC struck a US airbase in Bahrain, and the Kremlin announced a surprise Putin-Xi-Trump trilateral in Shenzhen on November 19. That last one alone reshapes expectations about every active conflict on the board.

items.title: FAA Ground Stop: Controllers Reject the Official Story
items.blurb: Friday's nationwide flight ground stop — only the third in US history, affecting an estimated 1.5 million travelers — now has controllers on record contradicting Transportation Secretary Duffy's explanation that overloaded switches caused inconsistent radar data. A reporter says she spoke with 60 controllers and none believed the official account. The gap between what institutions say after infrastructure failure and what the people inside them saw is widening.

items.title: PancakeSlicer: Non-Planar Slicing That Actually Ships
items.blurb: Non-planar FDM has been theoretically promising for years; Zimeng Xiong's PancakeSlicer is a working implementation for standard 3-axis printers — tested on a Bambu A1 Mini — that eliminates top-surface stair-stepping by tracing rays through the part to find printable surfaces and continuously morphing layer thickness. The cooling shroud swap for a remote static system is a clever enabler. This is the finish-quality gap that has kept FDM out of professional output closing in real time.

items.title: Prusa INDX After 40,000 Tool Changes
items.blurb: CNC Kitchen is the most rigorous stress-tester in desktop fabrication — the channel that actually runs the numbers and breaks the machines. His verdict after 40,000 tool changes on the INDX is 'a mess, but I love it': that specific tension between mechanical ambition and real-world reliability is exactly what you want to hear before deciding whether a category-defining machine belongs in your shop.

items.title: Burial Archaeology and the Moment Inequality Became Hereditary
items.blurb: Researchers used a tool called QuantWealth to score nearly 300 Corded Ware graves from ancient Bohemia (2900–2300 BCE) on factors like manufacturing time, scarcity, and distance of origin — and watched, in the grave goods, the precise historical moment when accumulated advantage started compounding across generations. The genetics of the deceased were also sequenced, tracking how steppe migration intersected with the emerging inequality gradient. Burial archaeology as the original ledger of status.

items.title: A Dead Star Pulsing Every 8 Minutes — With a Sun-Like Companion
items.blurb: Long-period radio transients — objects that flash bright radio pulses every few minutes to hours — were already strange; the assumed pattern was white dwarf paired with a small, cool red dwarf. This new one, found with the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia, has a companion that looks like our own Sun, breaking the emerging model before it was even fully established. An 8-minute clock on a dead star with no good physical explanation for how it keeps time.

items.title: An MP3 Player Built Entirely Inside Factorio
items.blurb: Nablanaut built a fully functional MP3 player inside Factorio using only the game's in-game speaker elements — no mods, just factory logic. The core problem is that Factorio's synth voices aren't discrete tones, so playing arbitrary audio required something like Fourier decomposition under severe constraints; the blueprint (generated procedurally by script) contains both the audio samples and playback logic. Watch the video for the moment the output goes from obviously wrong to genuinely recognizable — it's a demonstration that computation is substrate-independent, made unreasonably compelling.

facts.fact: The WHO's first-ever clinical guidelines for adult Type 1 diabetes were issued in November 2026 — more than 100 years after insulin's discovery, with roughly 9.5 million people currently living with the condition globally.

A Malaysian data center called A201 is legally supplying Nvidia AI compute to a Chinese tech giant by sitting outside China's borders — a loophole the Commerce Secretary, whose sons' firm counts A201's operator as a client, has reportedly been slowing efforts to close.

Columbia biomedical engineers built the first 3D stem cell models of early human placenta formation by briefly resetting pluripotent stem cells to a 'naive' state and suppressing the Hippo signaling pathway — the cells then self-organized over three weeks into chorionic tissue with fluid-filled lacunae mimicking early implantation.

Friday's FAA ground stop was only the third nationwide ground stop in US history, disrupting an estimated 1.5 million travelers and forcing airlines to cancel between 4,000 and 5,000 of approximately 41,000 scheduled flights.

art_picks.title: Upstream Color
art_picks.creator: Shane Carruth
art_picks.why: A film built entirely from systems — biological, psychological, economic — that the viewer has to assemble themselves; it treats the feedback loop between organisms and capital as something you feel before you understand, which is exactly the kind of deep structure under expressive surface that hooks you.

art_picks.title: Mycelium Studies / Spore Prints
art_picks.creator: Neri Oxman (MIT Media Lab Archive)
art_picks.why: Oxman's work is the rare case where biological systems, fabrication, and aesthetic obsession fuse into something genuinely category-less — not 'design inspired by nature' but actual structural computation borrowed from living organisms; the archive at the MIT Media Lab site documents the full process thinking, not just the objects.

art_picks.title: Vespertine
art_picks.creator: Björk
art_picks.why: One of the purest examples of a feedback loop as compositional architecture — microbeats, music boxes, and voice nested inside each other like Russian dolls; it functions as both intimate mythology and a sonic system, the kind of album that makes you want to design something.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt — Last Chance
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St
events.why: Freestanding screens in MoMA's outdoor garden showing AI-reconstructed images derived from fMRI brain scans, mutated in real time by visitors' gazes and simulated cancer-cell data — it's literally a nonhuman perceptual system made visible, and it closes the 29th.

events.name: James Turrell: Something Old, Something New, Something Borrowed, Something Blue
events.why: New Shallow Space and Glassworks pieces from Turrell — the person who went more unreasonably deep on a single perceptual question (what is light as architecture?) than almost anyone alive; small gallery, intimate scale.

events.name: Nairy Baghramian: nameless
events.why: Baghramian makes sculpture that is preoccupied with the edge between body and architecture, support and load — formal, strange, and genuinely hard to categorize; this is her first major New York showing in years.

events.name: artport: A History of Internet Art — Opening
events.venue: Whitney Museum of American Art, 99 Gansevoort St
events.why: The Whitney's browser-based gallery artport turns 25 and spills into physical galleries — over 100 net art works from JODI to Holly Herndon/Mat Dryhurst, structured to feel like floating browser windows; a rare institutional retrospective of the early internet as aesthetic frontier before it hardened.

events.name: Gnarls Barkley: To Whom It Still Concerns Tour
events.why: First tour in 18 years from one of the genuinely genre-dissolving acts of the 2000s — soul, hip-hop, indie rock, art-pop collapsed into one project — in a 1,000-cap room rather than an arena; note: verify ticket status directly on Live Nation before going, as one source flagged a potential cancellation.

trial_sources.name: Global Inequality and More 3.0 — Branko Milanovic
trial_sources.why: A world-class economist writing with rare range — geopolitics, empire, inequality, and intellectual history — at the precise intersection of current events and deep structural forces this reader craves.

trial_sources.name: Scott Carney's Substack
trial_sources.why: Investigative journalist and author (What Doesn't Kill Us) who surgically separates credible longevity/stem cell/peptide science from charlatanry — exactly the skeptical, primary-source lens this reader needs on health research.

trial_sources.name: Alex Danco's Substack
trial_sources.why: Writes with unusual precision on how ideas, tools, and social technologies spread — covering taste formation, community design, the aesthetics of software, and cultural capital in ways few others attempt.
